newsitem.title: USA: Five oil companies fight federal subpoenas.
newsitem.headline: Five oil companies fight federal subpoenas.

text.p: Five oil companies subpoenaed last fall by the U.S. government have refused to hand over records of oil sales from 1980 to 1988, a federal agency said Thursdday.
The records were sought in a dispute over whether the companies underpaid royalties they owed the U.S. government on oil they produced on federal land in California.

Chevron Corp., Mobil Corp., Occidental Oil and Gas Corp., Atlantic Richfield Co. and Royal Dutch/Shell's Shell Oil are fighting the subpoenas, U.S. Minerals Management Service Director Cynthia Quarterman told a news conference.
"We expect them to begin court action soon," she said.
Three other companies -- Exxon Corp., Unocal Corp. and Pennzoil Co. -- complied with the request by the agency, which is part of the Interior Department.

Last fall, the Minerals Management Service billed 10 companies -- including Unocal, Mobil, Occidental, Shell and ARCO -- for a total of $385 million in allegedly underpaid royalties on sales of oil from California offshore and onshore drilling sites leased from the federal government.
The oil companies argue that they have paid all the royalties they owed in the past, based on regulations in place at the time.
Under those rules, companies were expected to pay royalties based on the market value of their oil, which the government at the time said included companies' posted prices.
But, following a two-year study, the Mineral Management Service last year found that companies had sold their oil at premiums to posted prices.
"They paid us (based on) one thing, then paid themselves above that," said Robert Armstrong, assistant secretary for land and minerals management.
Sen. Barbara Boxer, a California Democrat, accused the companies of trying to get out of what they truly owe and of depriving California of about $75 million for public schools.
California receives 50 percent of royalties collected from federal leases in the state.
"It is outrageous that ... deadbeat oil companies still have not paid the bills sent to them by the federal government," she said at the news conference.

"If the companies would open their books, we could solve this," she said, adding that Shell, Mobil, USX-Marathon Group and Oryx Energy Co. were the worst offenders in terms of how much in royalties they owed.
